questions.stem: The recurrence relation for the number of operations performed by a divide-and-conquer algorithm that divides an array into two halves, sorts them separately, and then merges them is given by T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n). What is the solution to this recurrence in Big O notation?
questions.solution: The merge sort algorithm follows a divide-and-conquer strategy, where the time complexity for dividing and merging is O(n). The recurrence relation T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n) corresponds to the Master Theorem case 1 (a=2, b=2, c=1). Using the Master Theorem, we get a solution of O(n log n).
questions.explanation: The Master Theorem helps us analyze divide-and-conquer recurrences. In this case, since a = 2 and b = 2, the dominant term is n^(log_2(2))/log_2(2) = n, which gives O(n log n) as the solution.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to choose A (O(n)), which only accounts for the merging step and not the recursive calls. C (O(n^2)) is incorrect because it doesn't capture the logarithmic growth of the divide-and-conquer approach.

questions.stem: Given the recurrence relation T(n) = 3T(n/4) + O(1), where T(1) = O(1), what is the solution to this recurrence in Big O notation?
questions.solution: The recurrence relation T(n) = 3T(n/4) + O(1) corresponds to the Master Theorem case 3 (a=3, b=4, c<log_4(3)). Using the Master Theorem, we get a solution of O(log n).
questions.explanation: In this case, since a = 3 and b = 4, the dominant term is log_b(n) = log_4(3n/4), which becomes O(log n) as n approaches infinity. T(1) = O(1) ensures that the constant factor does not affect the overall time complexity.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be to choose B (O(n)), which is incorrect because it doesn't account for the decrease in problem size with each recursive call. C and D are wrong because they overestimate the growth rate of the recurrence.
